query: What target differential privacy parameters (epsilon, delta) are acceptable for on-device embeddings and aggregated signals, and how will we translate DP noise into an empirical re-identification risk metric?

response.query: What target differential privacy parameters (epsilon, delta) are acceptable for on-device embeddings and aggregated signals, and how will we translate DP noise into an empirical re-identification risk metric?
response.answer: For on-device embeddings and aggregated signals, epsilon typically ranges from 0.1 to 1, with delta often set to 10^-7 to balance privacy and utility. DP noise translates to re-identification risk via metrics like the L2-sensitivity and the privacy budget.

results.content: It covers a wide range of topics on the subject and provides comprehensive guidance for privacy auditing schemes based on privacy attacks to protect machine-learning models from privacy leakage. The integration of DP methods into ML models makes them more robust to privacy attacks and paves the way for differential private machine learning (DPML) [15,16,17,18]. To investigate and audit the privacy of data and models, you must first apply a specific type of attack, called privacy attack, to a DP algorithm and then perform an analysis, for example, a statistical calculation. To evaluate data leakage in ML, we categorize privacy attacks into membership inference attacks [51,52,53], data-poisoning attacks [54,55], model extraction attacks [56,57], model inversion attacks [58,59], and property inference attacks [60]. Recent research on privacy attacks for privacy auditing is categorized into five main categories: membership inference attacks, data-poisoning attacks, model inversion attacks, model extraction attacks, and property inference. results.title: AI Interview Mastery Series Day 4 — Trust by Design
results.content: # AI Interview Mastery Series Day 4 — Trust by Design: Governance, Ethics & Compliance for C‑Level Accountability. Responsible and ethical AI has become a critical focus for AI engineering roles at major tech companies (FAANG and beyond). As AI systems influence high-stakes decisions in finance, healthcare, hiring, and more, companies are expected to ensure these models are fair, transparent, and respect user privacy. Internal policies (like Google’s AI Principles) and industry frameworks (e.g. NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework) also push for fairness, accountability, transparency, and privacy in AI systems [3]. Consequently, technical interviews for senior AI roles increasingly include deep questions on ethical AI: detecting bias, ensuring fairness across demographics, explaining model decisions, preserving privacy (through techniques like differential privacy and federated learning), and complying with evolving AI guidelines. Dr. Adnan Masood is an Engineer, Thought Leader, Author, AI/ML PhD, Stanford Scholar, Harvard Alum, Microsoft Regional Director, and STEM Robotics Coach.
